props.title: American Buffalo
props.initialSlug: Three men plot a doomed rare coin heist

sections.content: American Buffalo represents a masterful adaptation of David Mamet's searing stage play, joining other powerful theater-to-film translations like Glengarry Glen Ross (1992) and Death of a Salesman (1985). Dustin Hoffman delivers a tour-de-force performance as Teach, a small-time hustler plotting a coin heist with shop owner Don (Dennis Franz). The film preserves Mamet's signature staccato dialogue while director Michael Corrente creates a claustrophobic atmosphere in the junk shop setting that amplifies the characters' desperation.

sections.content: The film belongs to a vital tradition of 90s independent crime dramas that explore the desperation of small-time criminals, alongside works like Trees Lounge (1996) and Buffalo 66 (1998). These films share a gritty authenticity and focus on working-class characters whose grandiose schemes mask profound personal failures. The confined setting becomes a pressure cooker for masculine aggression and betrayal. SUBHEAD: The Art of Theatrical Adaptation

While some critics dismissed American Buffalo as too stagey, it actually demonstrates how theatrical intensity can translate to screen power, much like Tape (2001) and Bug (2006). The film's contained location forces attention onto the psychological warfare between characters, with Hoffman and Franz's performances creating a masterclass in screen acting that builds to a devastating climax.
